conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because the postpartum period can bring a lot of unexpected emotions along with the joy.  

Everything we talk about today is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you in the past seven days. We’ll go through ten questions together; most take only a moment to answer, and we can pause at any time.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start, how have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things lately—has it felt easy, or has it been a struggle?

Honestly? It’s been a struggle. Most days nothing feels funny at all, and when people try to joke it just feels like too much effort to even smile. I still laugh once in a while—like yesterday my partner made a silly face at the baby and I chuckled—but it fades fast and I’m right back to feeling heavy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
As much as I can, I guess… but it doesn’t come easy. Even when something is genuinely funny, the laugh feels kind of flat and disappears right away.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to anything. I still go through the motions—like I’ll plan a walk or promise a friend I’ll meet for coffee—but the excitement I used to feel just isn’t there. I do it more because I “should” than because I want to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I do that a lot. Like if the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” I’ll replay every little thing—did I eat something that upset her through the milk, did I pick her up too fast, too slow? Rationally I know babies cry, but I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much every day. My mind races with “what-ifs” about the baby—what if she stops breathing, what if I drop her, what if the stroller tips. Most of the time there’s no real reason, but I can’t shut it off. I can talk myself down after a while, but the next wave just hits.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ll be sitting on the couch, everything quiet, and suddenly my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t breathe. It only lasts a couple of minutes, but it’s terrifying—like my body thinks there’s danger when nothing’s happening at all.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, definitely. Most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the sink’s full of dishes, laundry’s piled up, I haven’t showered, and I just want to sit on the floor and cry. I manage somehow, but it all feels overwhelming and heavier than it ever did before she was born.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t quit. I keep going over everything I might have messed up with her today, or I picture scary “what-if” scenes, and then I’m wide awake. I finally drift off, but I wake up a couple of times with my heart pounding and have to talk myself down again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the day, most days. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. I can still smile at the baby or answer a text, but the sadness is underneath everything, and some evenings it feels like I’ll never get back to the old, lighter version of me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I put her in the crib for a nap, closed the door, and just crumpled onto the hallway floor sobbing. I couldn’t even name what set it off—everything just felt too heavy and the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind. Just brief flashes—like when I’m rocking her at 3 a.m. and feel totally useless—where I think “what if I just weren’t here?” I’ve never made any plan or wanted to act on it; it’s more this scary, passing picture that pops up maybe once or twice in a week, and then I feel awful for even thinking it.

You've shared how most days feel wrapped in a heavy, gray cloud where laughter fades quickly and nothing sparks excitement anymore. Between constant worries about your baby's safety, sudden panic sensations, and nightly battles with racing thoughts, it's understandable that simple tasks feel overwhelming and tears come without warning. Feeling like you're merely "treading water" while caring for your infant can be exhausting and isolating, and the fleeting, frightening thought of not being here shows how desperately your mind is searching for relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes diminished ability to laugh and fleeting enjoyment, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete absence of anticipatory enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot') and gives vivid examples of attributing the baby's fussing to personal failure, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily racing anxious thoughts without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring multiple times in the past week with physical symptoms and no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily overwhelm and inability to manage routine tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to persistent anxious thoughts and physical symptoms, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the day, most days" with a sense of hopelessness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two clear crying episodes this week triggered by overwhelming feelings, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, unwanted suicidal thoughts that are distressing but without intent or plan, matching 'Sometimes'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS=26 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. She endorses <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the time, plus <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>concentration worries</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym> without intent, meeting <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset. <sym>Generalized anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> are comorbid. Item 10 score ≥1 mandates urgent safety assessment.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Develop written safety plan and 24/7 support contacts now
3. Discuss evidence-based treatment options (therapy, <med>SSRIs compatible with breastfeeding</med>)
4. Schedule daily check-ins with partner/family and remove potential means of self-harm
5. Begin gentle routine: 10-min outdoor walk, balanced meals, accept household help
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or brief mindfulness when <sym>panic</sym> rises
7. Arrange immediate therapist appointment for <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med>
8. Consider local <med>postpartum support group</med> or 1-800-PPD-MOMS warmline
9. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress after intervention
10. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale analogue interview

Symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily tearfulness
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care
- Persistent, intrusive “what-if” worries about infant safety; panic episodes (HR, SOB) without trigger
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by rumination
- Overwhelm, feeling “treading water,” functional impairment (self-care, household tasks)
- Passive suicidal ideation (fleeting “what if I weren’t here,” no plan/intent)

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for ≥2 weeks, onset after delivery.

Screening significance: High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; passive SI indicates elevated safety risk.

Recommendation: Urgent referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of treatment options.
